title: Preference Alignment
oneLiner: Alignment teaches a model which answers people prefer: collect 'this one is better' judgements, turn them into a score, and train the model to earn higher scores without going off the rails.

what.html:
After fine-tuning, a model follows instructions, but it doesn't know which of several possible answers is best. Alignment uses preferences: people (or an AI judge) compare two answers and pick the better one. These comparisons train a reward model that scores answers, and the model is then trained to get higher scores (RLHF), or trained directly on the comparisons (DPO).

Everyday versionTraining a new chef by tasting pairs of dishes and saying "this one's better", rather than writing perfect recipes. Over time the chef learns your taste. But if you always praise extra salt, they'll start oversalting everything: that's reward hacking.

why.html:
• It's what makes chat assistants helpful, honest and careful.
  • It explains failures like flattery, over-refusal and gaming the score.
  • Newer methods (DPO, GRPO) made alignment far cheaper.

how.title: Why go beyond SFT?
how.html: SFT copies example answers. Alignment teaches the difference between a good answer and a better one: helpful, honest and harmless.

how.title: Collect comparisons
how.html: Show two answers, pick the better one. Labellers agree only about 3 times in 4, so the data is noisy and needs clear guidelines.

how.title: Turn comparisons into a score
how.html: A reward model gives each answer a number. If the preferred answer scores 2 and the other 1, it predicts a 73% chance people prefer the first.

how.title: Practise and get scored (RLHF)
how.html: The model writes answers, the reward model scores them, and training pushes the scores up, minus a penalty for drifting too far from the original model.

how.title: Skip the scorer (DPO)
how.html: DPO trains directly on the pairs: make the preferred answer more likely and the rejected one less likely, relative to the original model. Simpler and stable.

how.title: Compare within a group (GRPO)
how.html: Ask the same maths question 8 times, check which answers are right, and reward the ones above the group average. Great for problems with checkable answers.

how.title: AI feedback with written rules
how.html: An AI judge follows a short list of principles to compare answers, making feedback cheaper and the rules visible. Any score can still be gamed.

example.html:
Reward to probability. Scores 2 and 1 differ by 1; σ(1) = 1 / (1 + e⁻¹) = 0.73. The model predicts people prefer the first answer 73% of the time.

Supplementary Pushing a score too hard eventually makes real quality drop, a pattern known as Goodhart's law: "when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure."

misunderstandings: The reward model knows the truth.
DPO doesn't need a reference model.
It compares against a frozen reference.
Higher reward always means a better answer.
takeaways: Preferences teach which answer is better: helpful, honest, harmless.
Reward model: P(chosen ≻ rejected) = σ(r_w − r_l) (σ(1) = 0.73).
RLHF: PPO on reward − β·KL to the reference.
DPO: direct loss on pairs; GRPO: group-normalised rewards, no critic.
RLAIF/Constitutional AI scale feedback; watch for reward hacking.
thirty: Alignment optimises models for human preferences (helpful, honest, harmless). Preference data: prompts with chosen/rejected responses from labellers following guidelines (≈65–80% agreement). Reward models are trained with Bradley–Terry: P(y_w ≻ y_l) = σ(r_w − r_l), loss −log σ(r_w − r_l) (rewards 2 vs 1 → 0.73). RLHF uses PPO to maximise reward − β·log(π/π_ref), keeping the policy close to the SFT reference; it needs policy, reference, reward and critic models. DPO derives a closed-form loss on preference pairs, −log σ(β[Δ_w − Δ_l]), needing only policy and reference (loss 0.693 at start). GRPO samples G answers per prompt and uses (r − mean)/std as advantage, no critic, ideal with verifiable rewards. RLAIF and Constitutional AI use AI judges following written principles. Risks: reward hacking (length-biased reward picks a long wrong answer), sycophancy, over-refusal, over-optimisation.
